recent_posts.title: Elio Struyf - Front Matter CMS, Demo Time
recent_posts.summary: Elio Struyf, Microsoft MVP and GitHub Star, discusses his developer tools built as VS Code extensions. Front Matter CMS started in 2019 as a way to manage markdown front matter for static site generators without vendor lock-in. Demo Time is a VS Code extension that lets conference speakers script live coding demos using YAML/JSON, with scenes, acts, and steps — eliminating the stress of live typing on stage. It also doubles as a learning tool, letting attendees replay demos step-by-step at their own pace. Elio also covers Ghostwriter Agents, an AI-interview-driven blog writing workflow that preserves the author's voice, and Voice Snippets, an upcoming tool for voice-driven computer commands. The conversation touches on open source monetization challenges, the ethics of AI-assisted cloning of existing products, and the growing role of voice interfaces in developer workflows.

recent_posts.title: Alem Tuzlak - Tanstack Dev Tools and Tanstack AI
recent_posts.summary: Alem Tuzlak, creator of TanStack DevTools and co-creator of TanStack AI, discusses his journey from running a dev agency to building open source tooling for the TanStack ecosystem. TanStack AI is positioned as a type-safe alternative to Vercel's AI SDK, offering a provider-agnostic interface for chat, image generation, video, audio transcription, and more. Key differentiators include compile-time type safety that maps models to their supported options and tools, transport-agnostic streaming, and AGUI protocol support for standardized agent-to-client communication. The adapter architecture was deliberately split by capability to keep the project scalable for a two-person team. Upcoming features include middleware support, MCP server integration, execution workflows with retry/fallback, and deeper observability through dev tools.

recent_posts.title: Storybook's Journey to a Faster and More Efficient Future
recent_posts.summary: The Storybook core team discusses the tool's evolution toward better performance and developer experience. Key improvements include migrating from Webpack to Vite for dramatically faster startup times, adopting lazy loading, slimming down the dependency tree, and moving to ESM-only in Storybook 10. The Component Story Format (CSF) evolved from imperative function calls to static exports (CSF3), enabling server-side static analysis without executing user code — a major performance win for large codebases with thousands of stories. The team also grew from 3 to 8 engineers, enabling more focused optimization work. Storybook is described as a companion app for developing, documenting, and visually testing UI components in isolation.

recent_posts.title: Security risks of using AI as a cross-language translation layer
recent_posts.summary: A discussion on the security and reliability risks of using AI as a translation layer between programming languages and ecosystems. The conversation explores how modern systems are inherently multi-language (Python, JavaScript, Java, WebAssembly), glued together by JSON over HTTP, and how this creates gaps between developer intent and actual knowledge of language semantics. The speaker argues that tools like Temper, a language that transpiles to multiple target languages, can reduce manual review burden, enable shared type definitions across system boundaries, and complement AI-generated code by applying traditional compiler methods to produce more reliable software.

recent_posts.title: Paolo Ricciuti - Svelte, TMCP
recent_posts.summary: A podcast interview with Paolo Ricciuti, a Svelte team maintainer at Mainmatter, covering Svelte 5's runes-based reactivity system, async/await in components, SvelteKit remote functions (RPC), and his TMCP library for building MCP servers. Paolo explains how Svelte 5 moved from compile-time reactivity to a signal-based model enabling TypeScript file usage and deep dependency tracking. He discusses the experimental async features and remote functions in SvelteKit that simplify server-client data loading with security considerations. He also covers TMCP, a lightweight alternative to the official MCP TypeScript SDK with modular transports and standard schema support, and ongoing work on custom renderers for Svelte to enable native and terminal rendering targets.

recent_posts.title: The Temper Approach: Uniting Programming Languages
recent_posts.summary: Mike Samuel, a former Google security engineer with 17 years at the company, discusses Temper, a programming language he founded a company around. The core idea is a language designed from the ground up to translate/transpile into many target languages, allowing developers to write a library once and support all programming language communities. Motivated by the challenge of maintaining parallel versions of security libraries across many languages at Google, Temper targets the familiar functional/object-oriented paradigm (TypeScript-like syntax) and aims to compile to languages like Java, JavaScript, Python, and C#. The key differentiator from approaches like Scala is that Temper was designed specifically with multi-runtime translation as the primary goal, making deliberate early design trade-offs to support many runtimes rather than being retrofitted.

recent_posts.title: Google Calendar’s Inception and the Path to Modern Web Security
recent_posts.summary: A conversation with a Google engineer who built Google Calendar in 2006 covers the early days of Ajax-era web development, the origins of the Closure Compiler as a just-in-time bundler for Gmail, and a pivot into web security engineering. The discussion explores the Kaha project, a programming language experiment applying object capabilities to browser security, aiming for mutual suspicion between independent code components. Lessons learned include the difficulty of imposing new languages on developer communities and the value of making security best practices the path of least resistance for developers and blue teams.

recent_posts.title: Ben Curtis - Honeybadger, Breakwater
recent_posts.summary: Ben Curtis, co-founder of Honeybadger, shares his journey from early web development and Rails adoption to building a bootstrapped error monitoring and observability platform over 14 years. He discusses the genesis of Honeybadger as a reaction to poor customer service from Airbrake, the decision to stay bootstrapped and avoid VC funding, and the technical evolution of the product including a custom query language (BadgerQL) and structured logging. Ben also introduces Breakwater, a new side project aimed at making it easy for software vendors to distribute and monetize Docker images with license-based access control. He offers advice for indie hackers around patience, personal motivation, and not underestimating marketing, and explains Honeybadger's 30-hour work week philosophy.

recent_posts.title: Jamon Holmgren - Infinite Red, Into the Dawn
recent_posts.summary: Jamon Holmgren, co-founder and CTO of Infinite Red, shares his journey from tinkering with DOS batch files at age 11 to running a 32-person React Native consultancy for a decade. He discusses how Infinite Red became early React Native adopters starting at version 0.11, built the Ignite starter kit, Chain React conference, and React Native Radio podcast. He reflects on the evolution of React Native from rough early days to the current Expo-dominated era, and how the new architecture continues to accelerate adoption. Jamon also talks about building a co-op combat helicopter game called 'Into the Dawn' in Godot, initially vibe-coded with GPT-4 but later rewritten by hand after losing understanding of the codebase. He draws parallels between Godot's hot-reload and React Native's architecture, and explains how game dev thinking about frame-perfect performance influenced his approach to React Native optimization.
